description: A litigation director must approve the company's response to a subpoena seeking source code, pricing records, and internal communications in a trade-secret lawsuit, with input from e-discovery counsel, research counsel, and the client liaison.

shared_context.S1: The court has ordered the company to respond to the opposing party's subpoena within ten days.
shared_context.S2: The subpoena requests source-code files, pricing emails, and internal communications about the accused product.
shared_context.S3: The response may include document production, a motion for a protective order, and sealed filings.
shared_context.S4: Under the litigation team's routine response protocol, Maya Chen conducts a check-in with e-discovery, research, and client-relations personnel before approving the final response.

PF1.text: Owen completed a forensic review of the responsive source-code set this morning and found exactly 14 files: 9 contain current proprietary source code and 5 are obsolete sample files with no trade-secret content. The review results are still being uploaded to the discovery workspace, so they are not in the response draft yet.

PF2.text: Leila's research for a related motion found a controlling appellate decision requiring any subpoena production containing trade-secret material to be preceded by a sealed submission and a proposed protective order that expressly bars use of the material in expert training. She has not circulated the case because her research memorandum is awaiting citation checking.

PF3.text: During yesterday's client call, Sam confirmed that the client will authorize production of its non-trade-secret pricing emails only if the protective order requires destruction of all produced copies within exactly 30 days after the lawsuit ends. Sam recorded this in his call notes, which have not yet been added to the matter file.

acceptance_conditions: Exactly the 5 obsolete source-code files must be produced.
The 9 current proprietary source-code files must be withheld.
A sealed submission must precede any production containing trade-secret material.
The protective order must prohibit use of produced trade-secret material in expert training.
The non-trade-secret pricing emails must be produced.
The protective order must require destruction of all produced copies exactly 30 days after the lawsuit ends.
The controlling appellate decision must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: The subpoena identifies source-code files but not their condition; PF1 changes the production decision to exactly 5 obsolete files and withholding the 9 current proprietary files.
Without PF2, the response could omit a sealed pre-production submission and the exact protective-order prohibition on expert training.
The client will permit pricing-email production only when the protective order sets copy destruction at exactly 30 days after the lawsuit ends.
